rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.
Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to probe selectivity in the critical central cluster. The first run has ample time margin, so improving the R = 0.51 pair is the priority.

Use a shallower gradient at the best temperature to improve the remaining critical pair, exploiting the substantial margin below 10 minutes. Further heating risks compressing another central pair whose resolution fell from 4.77 to 2.07.

The shallower gradient worsened the closest pair, indicating a selectivity limitation rather than simple crowding. Raise temperature another 5 C to separate that pair, with a modestly longer gradient to protect the neighboring pair that narrowed on heating.

Lengthen the gradient by one grid step to improve the new limiting pair at R = 1.29. This small adjustment may retain sufficient separation in the R = 1.61 pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Injection 5 achieved the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek earlier elution while testing whether full resolution survives the narrower gradient window.

Test a lower starting organic fraction with the shorter gradient to recover the central separation that failed in injection 4. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved method while retaining injection 5 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Shorten injection 7's gradient by one step to test the speed limit for full resolution. Its two tight pairs leave little margin, so retain injection 7 as the faster maximum-score benchmark if separation deteriorates.

Test the upper temperature limit with the shorter gradient to determine whether a selectivity change can restore full resolution at faster elution. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity, since heating the short gradient caused a different central pair to co-elute. The original run's time margin makes this a reasonable test for an alternative fully resolved, short-gradient method.

Test whether higher starting organic moves the temperature-sensitive central pair beyond its co-elution point and restores separation in reversed order. This also seeks faster elution, while checking whether the early peaks remain sufficiently retained and resolved.

Lower the starting organic fraction to recover early-pair resolution, and shorten the gradient to test separation of the central pair after its order reversal. This probes a faster alternative while preserving the confirmed maximum-score methods.

Shorten the gradient one step to test whether the reversed central pair gains enough selectivity to reach R = 1.5. Monitor its neighboring pair closely, since its current R = 1.62 leaves little margin for compression.

Lower temperature at the promising eight-minute gradient to move the central pair away from its high-temperature co-elution region. The higher starting organic fraction and steeper gradient may preserve separation of the other temperature-sensitive pair.

Test a shallower gradient at 40 C for an alternative selectivity window, since the critical cluster changes elution order between 40 and 50 C. Lower starting organic should protect early separation, while the high endpoint limits the risk of unobserved late peaks.

Lower temperature by 5 C to move the remaining close pair away from its apparent order-crossing region, while shortening the gradient to reduce late elution. Check the neighboring central pairs for compensating losses in resolution.

Return to the fastest fully resolved conditions, preserving injection 7's gradient slope but reaching the endpoint two minutes sooner. All peaks previously eluted before this new endpoint, so this shorter programmed gradient should retain the maximum CRF.

Refine between the successful 14-minute and under-resolved 12-minute gradients at this starting composition by lowering the endpoint. The intermediate slope should preserve full resolution while eluting the last peak earlier than injection 5.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 18 to test the faster boundary of full resolution. The limiting central pair may approach R = 1.5, so retain injections 7 and 17 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score methods.

Increase injection 17's endpoint by one step to test a modestly steeper gradient between the resolved and under-resolved conditions. This directly probes whether the fastest confirmed maximum-score method can be shortened further without losing central-pair resolution.
Use an intermediate slope between injections 18 and 19 to target full resolution near the faster boundary. This should improve the R = 1.47 pair while keeping the last peak earlier than injection 18.

Lengthen injection 6's gradient one step to recover its limiting central pair while retaining the improved separation of the other critical pair. This tests a potentially more robust maximum-score alternative, with the last peak expected to remain below 10 minutes.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 22 to raise its R = 1.41 pair above 1.5 while preserving the other critical pair's margin. The last peak is expected around 9 minutes, allowing full resolution without a time penalty.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 23 to shorten elution while retaining its improved critical-pair margins. This lies between the fully resolved slope of injection 23 and the under-resolved slope of injection 22.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving the slope of the fastest confirmed fully resolved methods, injections 7 and 17. The endpoint should still occur after all peaks elute, so maximum CRF and approximately 7.6-minute last-peak elution are expected.
